title: A project can be deferred by a ruling without reading as stuck
ask: The program owner found, working replay-phase-b, that HQ has no way to distinguish a project waiting on a scheduled event by the CES ruling from one that is genuinely stuck. replay-phase-b is deferred by the 2026-09-02 no-fresh-recruiting ruling until the next release nears — nothing impedes it — yet status blocked reads as five-alarm trouble and (were it critical) would false-alarm the release train. Proposal: a status like deferred that carries its wake trigger, counts as neither fire nor a routeless blocker, but stays visible with its trigger shown. This changes what the CEO sees on the das
first_action: Read compute_signals in hq/server.py for every place status==blocked is tested, and hq/data/projects/replay-phase-b.json, then draft the status semantics for the CEO to rule on.

result:
Read every place HQ tests `status == "blocked"`, then wrote the ruling and the spec behind it.

**What I found.** The 2 September playtesting ruling parked two projects on one event — the green-tester sitting before the next public release scores the last onboarding bar *and* produces the human session the replay-verification work needs. HQ has no status for that, so the two ends of the same wait wear opposite wrong labels: the replay project says `blocked`, the onboarding-gate project says `planned`.

`blocked` is the expensive one. Every blocked project's unblock sentence becomes an entry in your dashboard queue, so before I filed this, the first line on your dashboard read *"record one never-before-played tester's first unguided session…"* — an instruction to go do the thing you ruled should not happen yet. Its blocked-since date also feeds the "nothing stuck over a week" check, which turns Product amber on 8 September for a wait you ordered. If a *release-critical* project were parked this way it would also enter the release train's risk list and false-alarm Player Update 1. `planned` is the quieter error: it reads as ready to start and hides the wait completely.

**What I changed.** A decision card for you, and the drafted semantics behind it in the designer queue: a fifth project status, `deferred`, carrying the decision that chose the wait, the event that ends it, and — the part that earns it — that event bound to something HQ can watch on its own, so a wait that outlives its trigger becomes a fire instead of a quiet row. Deferred work leaves your queue and the stuck clock but keeps its row on the program report reading *waits for the next public release*. The queue entry spells out all five rules and every place in the code that changes. Your dashboard's top line is now the card itself.

I did not re-tag the two projects or touch the dashboard code — whether a scheduled wait gets to leave your queue is the thing being ruled, and doing it first would decide it.

follow_ups.title: Teach HQ the waiting status
follow_ups.first_action: In hq/server.py, exclude deferred projects from the blocked list in _compute_signals_now and from api_program's gating set, then add the stale-wait goal to hq/data/goals/product.json, following the five rules in the Q-90 queue entry.
follow_ups.why: The ruling only takes effect once the dashboard can tell a scheduled wait from a stuck one.

follow_ups.title: Re-tag the parked projects and sweep the rest
follow_ups.first_action: Set the replay-verification and onboarding-gate project files to the waiting status with their wake triggers, then read the other thirteen project files for waits currently wearing planned or blocked.
follow_ups.why: Two projects are mislabelled today and the same ruling will park more before each release.

follow_ups.title: Decide how a wait reads on the dashboard and the program page
follow_ups.first_action: Choose the word and row treatment for a waiting project — the dashboard's in-flight/blocked chip, and the program page's Blocked tab heading, which would then cover rows it does not describe.
follow_ups.why: A third status changes what the CEO's glanceable counts mean, which is her charter.

recommend.question: Should work that is waiting on an event you scheduled still count as blocked?
recommend.answer: No — rule for the third status, with the event that wakes it recorded and watched.
recommend.why: Until it lands, your dashboard's top line tells you to do the thing you ruled should not be done yet, and the Product pillar goes amber on 8 September for a wait you ordered.
recommend.instead: Keep one blocked status and snooze the two projects until a date — half the work, but blocked keeps meaning two different things and somebody has to re-pick the date every time it lapses.

check.summary: Sofia did exactly the asked step — the deferred-status semantics are drafted in the queue and a clean decision card is on the inbox, with every code claim (Eye of Sauron entry, blocked-too-long clock, release-train gating set) checked out true — but the amber date she gives you is one day early.

findings.what: The card and queue entry say Product goes amber on 8 September; the goal is green while days-blocked is at or under 7, so a 2026-09-01 blocked_since first reads amber on 9 September (and 'in four days' should be five).
findings.where: hq/data/decisions/Q-90.json (question, why_now, option c); docs/DESIGNER_QUEUE.md Q-90 entry
findings.fix: Change the date to 9 September in all four places, or drop the specific date and say 'later this week'. Owner: sofia.

findings.what: The queue entry leans on internal names — Eye of Sauron, _compute_signals_now, api_program's gating set — which the card avoids; fine as the implementer's spec, but the queue is a CEO-facing doc per WRITING.md.
findings.fix: Acceptable as-is since the card carries the plain-language version; if anyone reworks the entry, fold the code names into a parenthetical 'where in the code' line at the end rather than the narrative.
